items.name: Altmann — the Klimt paintings come home
items.citation: Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677 (2004); Austrian arbitration award, 16 January 2006
items.court: US Supreme Court; arbitration panel in Vienna
items.work: Five paintings by Gustav Klimt, including the golden portrait Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), from the Vienna collection of Ferdinand and Adele Bloch-Bauer.
items.happened: Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer, a Jewish sugar industrialist, fled Austria after the Anschluss in 1938; his property was seized and the Klimts ended up in Austria's national gallery, the Belvedere. His niece Maria Altmann, by then living in California, claimed the paintings under Austria's restitution law in 1998 and was refused. Suing in Austria would have meant a court filing fee set as a percentage of the paintings' value — initially over a million dollars — so she sued Austria instead in federal court in California.
items.question: Could a foreign government be sued in an American court, under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976, over property it had taken decades before that Act existed?
items.outcome: Yes. The Supreme Court held in 2004 that the Act's expropriation exception applied to the earlier taking, so Austria enjoyed no immunity. Rather than face a trial in Los Angeles, both sides agreed to binding arbitration in Austria. In January 2006 the arbitrators decided that Ferdinand, not Adele, had owned the paintings — Adele's will had expressed a wish, not a binding bequest — and that his heirs therefore owned them. Austria returned all five paintings in March 2006, 67 years after the seizure and eight years after the claim began.
items.matters: Altmann proved that American courts could be a realistic forum against foreign states — and that the credible threat of a US trial could push a government into a fair process at home. It also showed the limit of that route: the Supreme Court decided only that Austria could be sued, not who owned the paintings; the art itself was won from Austrian arbitrators applying Austrian law. Months after the return, Adele Bloch-Bauer I sold for $135 million, then the highest price ever paid for a painting; it hangs in the Neue Galerie in New York.
items.sourceName: Case note, Art-Law Centre, University of Geneva (ArThemis)

items.name: Cassirer — the Pissarro still in Madrid
items.citation: Cassirer v. Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation, 596 U.S. 107 (2022); Supreme Court order vacating and remanding, 10 March 2025
items.jurisdiction: United States (over a painting held in Spain)
items.court: US Supreme Court; US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
items.work: Camille Pissarro, Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon, Effect of Rain (1897), now in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid.
items.happened: In 1939 Lilly Cassirer Neubauer was forced to hand the painting to a Nazi-appointed dealer, for a sum paid into a blocked account she never touched, as the price of permission to leave Germany. The painting passed through dealers in the United States and was bought in 1976 by Baron Hans Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza; Spain later acquired his collection, and the painting has hung in Madrid since 1993. Lilly's grandson Claude Cassirer, living in California, sued the Spanish state foundation that owns the museum, in California, in 2005.
items.question: Before ownership could be argued at all, the courts had to choose the rulebook: under Spanish law, a holder who takes a work without knowledge of the theft can become its owner after a period of years; under California law, a thief can never pass good title. Which country's property law decides — and by what method is that choice made?
items.outcome: No party disputes that the painting was looted; the entire fight is about which law applies. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in 2022 that the lower courts had used the wrong method: California's choice-of-law rules, not a federal rule, should make the selection. Applying those rules, the Ninth Circuit still chose Spanish law in January 2024, so the museum kept the painting. California's legislature then amended its law in 2024 to require California substantive law in cases of this kind, including pending ones — and in March 2025 the Supreme Court set aside the 2024 judgment and sent the case back to be reconsidered under the new statute. Twenty years after the claim was filed, it remains undecided, and the painting remains in Madrid.
items.matters: Cassirer is the clearest modern demonstration that in restitution cases the procedural question — which law? — can matter more than the merits. It also shows a legislature intervening in a live case, and the constitutional and practical questions that raises. For claimants the lesson is sobering: a painting everyone agrees was looted can stay with its holder for decades while the legal system argues about which rulebook to open.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the US Supreme Court, 21 April 2022 (Cornell LII)

items.name: Philipp — the Guelph Treasure and the limits of American courts
items.citation: Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, 592 U.S. 169 (2021)
items.work: The Guelph Treasure (Welfenschatz): several dozen medieval reliquaries and devotional objects, now in the Kunstgewerbemuseum, Berlin.
items.happened: A consortium of Jewish art-dealing firms bought the treasure in 1929, just before the crash destroyed its resale value. In 1935 the dealers sold the remaining 42 pieces to the Prussian state for 4.25 million marks. Their heirs later said the price was about a third of the treasure's value and the sale coerced by Göring's agents at a time when Jewish dealers were being driven out of the trade. The heirs first went to Germany's Advisory Commission (the companion entry below), then sued Germany and its museum foundation in federal court in Washington, D.C.
items.question: A foreign state can be sued in the US over property only if the claim fits the expropriation exception to sovereign immunity — property 'taken in violation of international law'. Does a government's taking of property from its own citizens count as such a violation?
items.outcome: No. A unanimous Supreme Court held in February 2021 that the exception incorporates the 'domestic takings rule': the international law of expropriation governs takings from foreigners, not a state's treatment of its own nationals — and that is so even where the taking formed part of a genocide. The judgment that had allowed the case to proceed was vacated, and the claim against Germany could not go forward in the United States. The treasure remains in Berlin.
items.matters: Philipp closed the American courthouse to a large class of Holocaust-era claims — those against a foreign state for what it took from its own citizens, which describes a great share of Nazi takings from German Jews. Such claimants are thrown back on the processes of the country holding the work: in Germany's case an advisory commission whose recommendations bind no one, and which in this very dispute had already recommended against return.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the US Supreme Court (Justia)

items.name: The Guelph Treasure before Germany's Advisory Commission
items.citation: Recommendation of the Advisory Commission (Beratende Kommission), 20 March 2014
items.court: Advisory Commission on the return of cultural property seized as a result of Nazi persecution (the 'Limbach Commission')
items.work: The same Guelph Treasure as in Philipp — one dispute seen from both sides of the Atlantic.
items.happened: The dealers' heirs and the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which holds the treasure, agreed to submit their dispute to the Advisory Commission Germany created in 2003 for such cases, chaired by Jutta Limbach, a former president of the Federal Constitutional Court. The Commission examined the 1935 sale in detail: the price, the state of the market, and whether the dealers had been put under pressure.
items.question: Was the 1935 sale a forced sale caused by Nazi persecution, so that the Washington Principles' call for a 'just and fair solution' required the treasure's return?
items.outcome: The Commission said no. It found the price was within the range achievable on the severely depressed art market of the time; that the sellers received the agreed price at their free disposal; that the treasure had been outside Germany since 1930, beyond the regime's reach; and that there was no evidence the dealers were pressured in the negotiations. It recommended against restitution. The recommendation is not legally binding — but the Foundation followed it, and the heirs' remaining route was the American lawsuit that ended in Philipp.
items.matters: This is the German model in action: expert, reasoned, public, and far cheaper than litigation — but advisory only, available only where the holding institution agrees to take part, and final in practice because there is no appeal. Critics observe that asking whether this particular sale was coerced, document by document, sets a high evidential bar for events ninety years old; supporters answer that the Commission decides on evidence rather than presumption. Either way, the claimant's fate rests on persuasion, not on an enforceable right.
items.sourceName: Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, press release, 20 March 2014 (PDF)

items.name: Bakalar — right about title, beaten by the clock
items.citation: Bakalar v. Vavra, 619 F.3d 136 (2d Cir. 2010); judgment for the possessor on laches affirmed, 2012
items.court: US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit; US District Court for the Southern District of New York
items.work: Egon Schiele, Seated Woman with Bent Left Leg (Torso), a drawing from the collection of the Viennese cabaret artist Fritz Grünbaum.
items.happened: Grünbaum was arrested in 1938, made to sign a power of attorney while imprisoned in Dachau, and died there in 1941; his wife Elisabeth was murdered in 1942. His collection of 449 works, including 81 Schieles, disappeared. In 1956 Grünbaum's sister-in-law sold a group of Schiele works to a Swiss gallery; this drawing passed to New York, where the collector David Bakalar bought it in good faith in 1963 for $4,300. The title question surfaced only in 2004, when Bakalar consigned the drawing to Sotheby's and the sale was frozen. Bakalar sued to confirm his ownership; the Grünbaum heirs counterclaimed.
items.question: Two questions in sequence: whose law decides ownership — Switzerland's, which can give a good-faith buyer good title, or New York's, under which a thief passes no title at all? And even under New York law, had the heirs waited so long that the equitable defence of laches — unreasonable delay that prejudices the other side — barred them?
items.outcome: The Second Circuit held in 2010 that New York law applied, not Swiss law. On remand, the district court found in 2011 that Bakalar had not proved good title — the chain back to Grünbaum's sister-in-law did not show she had any right to sell the drawing — but that the heirs' claim was barred by laches in any event: decades had passed, and witnesses who might have explained the 1956 sale were dead. The Second Circuit affirmed in 2012. Bakalar kept the drawing; the heirs recovered nothing.
items.matters: Bakalar is the cautionary counterweight to Reif, which concerned the same collection: in New York a claimant can be right about ownership and still lose to delay. Laches cuts cruelly in Nazi-era cases, because the delay was itself caused by the persecution — the owners were murdered, the records scattered — yet the defence asks what the claimant did with the years since. The case also marks the fork created by choice of law: had Swiss law governed, the good-faith purchaser would likely have won on title outright, without any need to plead delay.
items.sourceName: Case note, Art-Law Centre, University of Geneva (ArThemis)

items.name: Reif v. Nagy — the Schiele works returned
items.citation: Reif v. Nagy, 175 A.D.3d 107 (Appellate Division, First Department, 2019)
items.court: Supreme Court, New York County (2018), affirmed by the Appellate Division, First Department (2019)
items.work: Egon Schiele, Woman in a Black Pinafore (1911) and Woman Hiding Her Face (1912), also from Fritz Grünbaum's collection.
items.happened: The London dealer Richard Nagy acquired the two works in 2013. The Grünbaum heirs learned in 2015 that he held them, demanded their return, were refused, and sued in New York in 2016. The evidence showed the works had been Grünbaum's, had been inventoried by a Nazi-appointed trustee, and had never been voluntarily transferred by Grünbaum or his estate.
items.question: Could the heirs prove their title on evidence that was partly circumstantial, and did delay — the defence that had defeated the same family in Bakalar — bar this claim too?
items.outcome: The heirs won outright. The trial court gave them summary judgment in 2018, and the Appellate Division affirmed in July 2019: Grünbaum had been dispossessed through persecution, no voluntary transfer was shown, and under New York law a thief passes no title to anyone downstream. Laches failed because Nagy had bought the works only in 2013, knowing of the heirs' claims to the Grünbaum collection, and had lost no evidence in the short interval before the demand. The works were ordered returned to the heirs.
items.matters: Read with Bakalar, Reif maps the real battlefield in American cases: rarely the events of 1938, which are usually undisputed, but delay and the buyer's position. A buyer of fifty years' standing was protected by equity; a recent buyer who knew of the claim had no equity to protect. The court also read the federal HEAR Act as a statement of policy in favour of deciding such claims on their merits. For one family and one collection, American law thus produced opposite results — decided by the calendar and the purchaser, not by the history.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the Appellate Division, First Department (New York State Courts)

items.name: Vineberg — the Stern estate's sixty-year search
items.court: US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
items.work: Franz Xaver Winterhalter, Mädchen aus den Sabiner Bergen ('Girl from the Sabine Mountains'), from the Düsseldorf gallery of the Jewish art dealer Dr Max Stern.
items.happened: The Nazi authorities ordered Stern, as a Jew, to liquidate his gallery. In November 1937 its stock was auctioned at the Lempertz auction house in Cologne at prices well below value, and Stern fled Germany. The Winterhalter was bought at that sale by Dr Karl Wilharm and remained in his family's private collection, almost never exhibited, for more than sixty years; his stepdaughter Maria-Louise Bissonnette inherited it and brought it to Rhode Island. Stern himself had searched for his pictures for decades and recovered some; his estate, working with the Art Loss Register and Germany's Lost Art database, located the painting when it was consigned for auction in 2004.
items.question: Ownership was barely contested. The appeal turned on laches: had the estate delayed so unreasonably, and so prejudiced the possessor, that its claim should be barred despite the forced sale?
items.outcome: The First Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the estate in November 2008, and the painting was ordered returned. Laches failed on the facts: the Stern side had searched diligently for decades, against records partly destroyed by bombing, while the possessor — who did not dispute that the painting came from the forced sale — could show no real prejudice from the delay.
items.matters: Vineberg is the working counter-example to Bakalar: laches is not automatic merely because a claim is old. Where the claimant can document a lifetime of searching, and the possessor cannot point to evidence lost through that delay, an American court will still reach the merits — and on the merits a sale ordered by the Nazi authorities gave the buyer no title the family was bound to respect. Note what made the difference: paperwork. Stern's documented searches were his estate's strongest evidence.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (FindLaw)

items.name: Guggenheim v. Lubell — New York's demand-and-refusal rule
items.citation: Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation v. Lubell, 77 N.Y.2d 311 (1991)
items.work: A gouache by Marc Chagall, stolen from the Guggenheim Museum in New York — an ordinary theft, not a Nazi-era case, included because it settled the rule that governs stolen-art claims in New York to this day.
items.happened: The gouache was stolen from the museum, apparently by a mailroom employee, in the late 1960s. The museum did not report the theft or publicise the loss. Jules and Rachel Lubell bought the work in 1967 from a well-known Madison Avenue gallery and displayed it in their home for more than twenty years. When the museum finally learned where the work was and demanded it back in 1986, Mrs Lubell refused, arguing that the museum's time to sue had expired long before, because it had never made any effort to look for its property.
items.question: When does the limitation clock start for an owner suing a good-faith buyer — at the theft, when the owner discovers the work, or only when the owner demands its return and is refused?
items.outcome: The Court of Appeals held in 1991 that in New York the clock starts at demand and refusal: until then the owner's claim has not even come into existence, and the owner is under no legal duty to search diligently — although unreasonable delay may still be examined under the separate defence of laches. The case returned to the trial court and settled on the second day of trial in 1993: Mrs Lubell kept the painting, and she and the dealers who had sold it to her paid the museum more than $200,000.
items.matters: Demand-and-refusal makes New York the most owner-friendly major jurisdiction in the world for stolen art: a claim can sleep for decades and wake intact the day the work surfaces. That is a principal reason so many Nazi-era cases are steered into New York courts, and why this theft case sits at the foundation of restitution law. The settlement teaches the companion lesson: even holding the winning rule, the museum took money and left the painting where it hung — sympathy for an innocent buyer, and the risks of trial, shape real outcomes as much as doctrine does.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the New York Court of Appeals (Cornell LII)

items.name: Von Saher — the Cranachs and the acts of the Dutch state
items.citation: Von Saher v. Norton Simon Museum of Art at Pasadena, 897 F.3d 1141 (9th Cir. 2018)
items.court: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
items.work: Lucas Cranach the Elder, Adam and Eve (c. 1530), two panels from the Amsterdam gallery of the Jewish dealer Jacques Goudstikker.
items.happened: Goudstikker fled the Netherlands in May 1940, leaving more than 1,200 works behind, and died in an accident during the voyage. His gallery was sold under duress to Hermann Göring's agent Alois Miedl. After the war the panels were recovered and handed to the Dutch state. Goudstikker's widow, on legal advice, did not file the Dutch restitution claim the post-war rules required within the deadline, and the Dutch courts later refused to restore her rights. In 1966 the Dutch government sold the panels to a collector, who sold them in 1971 to the Norton Simon Museum in California. In the 2000s the Dutch state returned to Goudstikker's heir, Marei von Saher, the more than 200 works it still held — but the Cranachs were in Pasadena, so she sued there.
items.question: Could an American court grant the claim without declaring invalid the official acts of the Dutch government — its post-war handling of the claim, its courts' refusal to restore rights, and its own sale of the panels in 1966?
items.outcome: No. After eleven years of litigation and three journeys to the Ninth Circuit, the court held in 2018 that the act of state doctrine required the Dutch government's acts within its own territory to be treated as valid; on that footing the museum's title, derived from the Dutch sale, was good, and the museum kept the panels. The claim failed without the American court ever deciding the rights and wrongs of 1940, which no one disputed.
items.matters: Von Saher shows a third way such claims fail: not on time limits or choice of law, but on doctrines of respect between states. A post-war settlement by the victim's own government — even one produced by a missed deadline, and partly reversed two generations later — can bind the family's hands abroad. The case also exposes a structural limit of state restitution programmes: the Netherlands could return what it still held, but the works it had sold away in the meantime were beyond its power to give back.
items.sourceName: Opinion of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (Justia)

items.name: Gentili di Giuseppe — France annuls a 1941 sale
items.citation: Gentili di Giuseppe v. Musée du Louvre, Court of Appeal of Paris, 2 June 1999
items.court: Court of Appeal of Paris, reversing the Paris trial court
items.work: Five Italian paintings — by Moretto da Brescia, Bernardo Strozzi, Giambattista Tiepolo, Alessandro Magnasco and Rosalba Carriera — from the Paris collection of Federico Gentili di Giuseppe.
items.happened: Gentili di Giuseppe, an Italian Jewish collector living in Paris, died in April 1940, weeks before the German invasion; his children fled Paris because of the racial laws. In April 1941 a court-appointed administrator sold the collection at the Hôtel Drouot, ostensibly to pay an estate debt, and buyers acting for Hermann Göring acquired the five paintings. After the war they were recovered and placed in French national museums as MNR works — held in custody pending claims by their owners. The heirs claimed in 1997 and were refused; the trial court in 1998 treated the sale as a regular estate administration and sided with the museum.
items.question: Was the 1941 sale a lawful settlement of an estate's debts, or an act of spoliation — a disposal that happened only because of the anti-Jewish measures — and therefore void under France's ordinance of 21 April 1945, which nullified such acts from the outset?
items.outcome: The Court of Appeal held in June 1999 that the sale was spoliation: the administrator had been appointed precisely because the heirs had fled the racial laws, so the disposal fell within the measures the 1945 ordinance annulled. The five paintings were ordered returned to the family, and were returned.
items.matters: Gentili was the first judgment ordering French national museums to hand back MNR works, and it established that a formally regular sale — auctioneer, catalogue, court-appointed seller — can still be void as spoliation if persecution is the reason it happened at all. France's route nonetheless remained narrow: the heirs won because a 1945 law happened to nullify their category of sale, and for most other categories a restitution from a French public collection continued to require its own Act of Parliament, until the framework law of 2023 created a general mechanism.
items.sourceName: French Ministry of Culture, 'New approaches of art looting from the 1990s till today' (PDF)

items.name: The Benevento Missal — a panel, a legal bar, and a new Act of Parliament
items.citation: Reports of the Spoliation Advisory Panel, 2005 and 2010 (HC 448); Holocaust (Return of Cultural Objects) Act 2009
items.court: Spoliation Advisory Panel (advisory); return authorised under the 2009 Act
items.work: The Beneventan Missal: a 12th-century service book written in Beneventan script, from the chapter library of Benevento Cathedral in southern Italy.
items.happened: The Missal disappeared from Benevento amid the chaos of the Allied bombing in 1943. A British officer bought it from a second-hand bookseller in Naples in 1944; the British Museum acquired it at auction in 1947, in circumstances the Panel later found ought to have prompted questions, and it passed to the British Library in 1973. The cathedral chapter brought its claim to the UK's Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2004.
items.question: The Panel concluded that the Missal had most probably been looted and that the moral claim to its return was strong — but the British Library Act 1972 forbade the Library to dispose of anything in its collection. What is a recommendation worth against a statute?
items.outcome: In 2005 the Panel recommended return in principle, proposed a loan in the meantime (which fell through), and took the unusual step of recommending that the law itself be changed. Parliament obliged with the Holocaust (Return of Cultural Objects) Act 2009, which allows 17 named national collections to return objects lost in the Nazi era where the Panel recommends return and ministers agree. On the renewed claim, the Panel recommended return in September 2010, ministers endorsed it, and the Missal was handed over that November — the first return made under the Act.
items.matters: The Missal is the English model working exactly as designed — and it still took six years and an Act of Parliament. The Panel judges the moral strength of a claim, unembarrassed by limitation periods or technicalities of title; but its recommendations are not self-executing, and the case had to create the machinery — the 2009 Act — that every later return from an English national collection now uses. Note, too, the claimant: an Italian cathedral chapter, for a wartime taking unconnected with the Holocaust — the Panel's remit covers losses in the Nazi era broadly, and it applied that remit on the merits as it found them.
items.sourceName: Report of the Spoliation Advisory Panel (GOV.UK)

items.name: The Lewenstein Kandinsky — advice rejected, policy changed, painting returned
items.citation: Binding opinion of the Netherlands Restitutions Committee (2018); settlement and handover by the City of Amsterdam (2021–22)
items.court: Restitutions Committee (binding opinion); Amsterdam District Court (2020)
items.work: Wassily Kandinsky, Bild mit Häusern (Painting with Houses, 1909), from the collection of Emanuel Lewenstein of Amsterdam.
items.happened: The Lewenstein family's collection was sold at auction in Amsterdam in October 1940, five months into the German occupation, in circumstances that have never been fully clarified; the Stedelijk Museum bought the Kandinsky at that sale. The family, the museum and the City of Amsterdam — which owns the collection — jointly asked the Restitutions Committee for a binding opinion. In 2018 the Committee advised against return: the sale could not be viewed apart from the occupation, but it might also have flowed from the family's worsening finances before the invasion, and the museum had bought in good faith. The heirs went to court to escape the opinion; the Amsterdam District Court upheld it in December 2020, because the parties had agreed in advance to be bound.
items.question: In the Dutch 'balance of interests', how should a museum's interest in keeping a work be weighed against a family's loss of it under occupation — and what happens when the answer a binding process gives is one the country comes to regard as wrong?
items.outcome: The painting went back anyway — by politics, not by law. The 2018 opinion became the leading exhibit in a national reckoning: the Kohnstamm review of 2020 concluded that Dutch restitution policy had become too formalistic and short on empathy, and recommended returning works whose loss was involuntary unless the holder's claim was clearly the stronger. The government adopted the new approach. In August 2021 the City of Amsterdam announced it would return the Kandinsky without further committee proceedings, and the painting was handed to the heirs in March 2022.
items.matters: No case shows the advisory model's character more plainly. The Committee's opinion was binding, and a court enforced it — yet the practical outcome was reversed within three years because the political system changed the standard the Committee applied, and claimants in the Netherlands have since faced a materially more generous test. Panel systems are quicker, cheaper and more humane than litigation, and they can correct themselves without a lawsuit on the merits; but this case is the standing reminder that what they give is policy, not rights, and policy can move in either direction.
items.sourceName: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, news report of the handover
